analysis.title: 2027 Global Outlook - AI's next chapter
key_insights: AI remains the dominant investment story, but the debate has moved from the size of the opportunity to its sustainability as tech groups use cash and debt to fund data-centre build-out.
L&G sees markets as fragile: higher interest rates, Middle East tensions, turbulent domestic politics and fiscal sustainability concerns (France) collide.

L&G's Bubble Index covers credit expansion, macro conditions and disruptive change, speculative behaviour, valuations and asset-price patterns. The first two flash warnings. The CIO judges the other three show the market is not yet in bubble territory.
Sentiment does not show widespread euphoria. Most hyperscalers have de-rated, in some cases significantly, and non-profitable tech has recently underperformed.

US real GDP growth is expected just above 2% in 2026, helped by AI investment. Europe is expected to grow little more than 1% because of exposure to natural gas prices and limited fiscal support. China is on track to hit its growth target.
Consensus 2027 growth forecasts have changed little despite higher inflation and rates. Unemployment is steady near full employment with very limited signs of AI disruption.

Growth risks are balanced. Downside: further energy price rises, the French presidential election (first round April 2027) and sovereign debt stress spreading to the European periphery, and AI debt issuance widening credit spreads and hurting equities and the consumer through wealth effects.

Upside risks: resolution of the Strait of Hormuz disruption, renewed asset price gains from AI productivity, and fewer central bank hikes than priced, especially in the UK. L&G sees the last as most likely.
Hyperscalers have again revised up AI spending plans in the latest earnings reports. Large AI debt issuance funds it.

AI's next phase may be set by energy supply, political response and geopolitics more than by the technology. Power supply and transmission are a major bottleneck, and tighter financial conditions are forcing more elaborate financing structures.

Local opposition to US data-centre construction is raising project costs and timelines. Democratic wins in key gubernatorial midterm races raise the prospect of some political brakes, but both parties support US leadership over China in AI, so the debate is about how to build, not whether.

Cloud demand underpins infrastructure demand at almost two-thirds of the total, growing at a 23% CAGR, rising to 40%+ with AI demand (Epoch AI). Infrastructure vacancy is at record lows, and new capacity takes five to ten years to build.

Unlike the early-2000s server and fibre boom, most new infrastructure is built to order, and data-centre development yields and cap rates have stayed strong and stable. BIS research warns the boom could still produce overcapacity.

For portfolios, L&G argues against treating AI as a binary bet. It favours firms with strong balance sheets and demonstrable revenue, separating exposure to adoption from exposure to current valuations, and diversifying across infrastructure providers and AI users.

Market pricing moved from about 50bps of 2026 easing at the start of the year to almost 100bps of hikes over 12 months, driven by the Middle East conflict, AI capex and stalled disinflation. After September's 25bps hike, the market prices about 80bps more over 12 months.

L&G thinks the Fed will deliver less than priced, limiting the cycle to reversing the 2025 insurance cuts, and has turned more constructive on short and intermediate US Treasuries. Core inflation has probably peaked. Real yields account for more than 90% of the rise in the 10-year yield since the Iran war began.
The consumer lacks tax cuts or a high saving rate to cushion higher rates and energy costs this time.

France's recent spread widening came from higher global yields and debt-servicing costs, not a new political shock. The fiscal tightening needed to stabilise debt/GDP is exceptionally large. Other sovereign spreads have started to rise.
ECB communication has turned more dovish, which should temper European yield rises relative to others and could make further ECB hikes difficult, increasing US-Europe rate divergence.
L&G has introduced French curve flatteners against Germany, on the view that France may cap how far European yields can rise. L&G states these positions may change and are not recommendations.

EM spreads widened on higher and more volatile US rates, a stronger dollar, high oil and weaker risk sentiment, but market access is intact, FX reserves are near records and sovereign rating momentum is positive. L&G sees the repricing as a rotation to quality and favours relative value over broad EM beta.

Energy security: gas has shown exposure to severe price swings, and countries less dependent on gas (such as Spain) proved more resilient. L&G argues decarbonisation and electrification strengthen energy security. The EU aims to raise electricity's share of final energy use from 23% to 46% by 2040.
The investable energy-security theme spans renewable generation, equipment makers, hydrogen, grids, smart-grid technology and storage. Clean-energy supply chains are concentrated in China.
DC pensions: focus is shifting from accumulation to retirement income. Sequencing risk in early retirement matters, and solutions need to combine flexibility, income and protection.

Retail participation has risen from about 8% of cash-equity volume to peaks of 25-30%. Leveraged ETF assets hit a record $218B in 1H 2026, more than 4.5x the 2020 level. SK Hynix is cited as an example of derivative flows amplifying price moves.

Equities overtook housing as a share of US household wealth for the first time in 15 years. Bottom-50% household equity and fund ownership is up over 570% since 2010. Retail crowding in momentum names risks sharp reversals, and recent weeks have seen big momentum swings.

DB pensions: higher yields have put many UK and US plans into surplus. Options include buyout, run-on or hibernation. Cashflow-driven investing and splitting liability and surplus portfolios are emphasised, and tight corporate spreads make credit less attractive.

Surprise 1, US Treasury reckoning: L&G estimates the US must shrink its deficit by 5% of GDP over a decade to stabilise debt/GDP. Such adjustments have happened only four times in 45 years among advanced economies. If it looks politically impossible, Treasuries could come under pressure and alternative safe havens could benefit.

Surprise 2, benign rotation out of AI winners: AI capex/GDP of 3-4% (2027E) rivals past booms. A rotation could occur gently as the AI ecosystem matures and earnings broaden, benefiting non-US equities and mid-risk assets.

Surprise 3, credit fragmentation: issuer dispersion is up since early 2026 (0.479 on 16 Oct 2026) while headline spreads stay tight. It is in the top quintile in Communications, Autos, Retailers and Financials ex-Banks, even excluding hyperscalers. Within-sector dispersion explained almost a third of year-to-year variation in median active manager alpha over 25 years.
Surprise 4, private investment-grade credit pays for complexity (bespoke collateral, uncertain funding dates, speed) rather than credit risk, for example chip financing with multiple delivery draws.
Surprise 5, real estate income resilience: income creation from tight-supply markets and asset operation can offset rate volatility.

sector_views.rationale: The boom may have further to run, but L&G prefers diversified exposure and strong balance sheets, and expects winners to differ from today's biggest spenders.
Electrification, grids and storage reinforce energy security and broaden the investable opportunity beyond generation.
Income creation in tight-supply markets can offset rate volatility, with upside if rates surprise positively.
Tight headline spreads mask rising issuer dispersion, which favours security selection.

earnings_insights: Latest hyperscaler earnings reports (per the report, no figures given) revised up AI capex plans again.
Most hyperscalers have de-rated, in some cases significantly, and non-profitable tech companies have recently underperformed.

risk_factors: Further energy price rises feeding a broader inflation shock.
French sovereign debt stress spreading to the European periphery.
AI debt issuance widening credit spreads and hurting equities and old-economy investment.
Higher equity share of US household balance sheets raising consumer sensitivity to equity declines.
Power and grid constraints, local opposition and tighter financing slowing the AI build-out.
Overcapacity if the AI boom outpaces demand, as the BIS warns.
US fiscal sustainability, with a possible Treasury market reckoning.
Retail leverage and momentum crowding amplifying reversals.
Hidden dispersion within credit markets under tight headline spreads.
charts_described: Epoch AI chart: AI-driven computation volume has expanded roughly five-million-fold since 2022, with a Q3 2026 estimate of 5.0M H100 equivalents.
Table of large fiscal adjustments: Sweden 1993-2006 at 10.5%, Canada 1981-2001 at 9.7%, Italy 1988-2000 at 8.2%, Spain 2008-2020 at 7.1% of GDP.
Table of historical capex booms: canals US 1840 1%, railways UK 1848 7%, electrification US 1928 1%, telecoms US 2000 1%, AI infrastructure US 2027E 3-4% of GDP.
Chart of relative issuer dispersion versus median annual active return, with latest dispersion at 0.479 on 16 October 2026.
vol_and_positioning: Retail share of cash-equity volume rose from about 8% to peaks of 25-30%.
Leveraged ETF assets reached a record $218B in 1H 2026, over 4.5x the 2020 level.
Single-stock leveraged ETFs and one-day options amplify moves, with SK Hynix cited as an example.
Retail crowding in momentum names means trend reversals can produce dramatic downside, and momentum swung sharply in recent weeks.
Sentiment indicators show no widespread euphoria.
Relative US IG issuer dispersion stood at 0.479 on 16 Oct 2026, in the top quintile in several sectors.
geopolitical: Middle East conflict and the Iran war, with disruption in the Strait of Hormuz, drove energy prices and rate expectations higher.
French presidential election first round in April 2027 adds to sovereign debt concerns.
US midterms and Democratic gubernatorial wins may bring political brakes on some data-centre development.
US-China competition in AI drives pressure to speed up chips, data-centre construction, permitting and energy access.
Frontier AI models can orchestrate mass cyber-attacks and may in future help design pathogens or weapons.
China dominance in solar panel, battery and power-electronics supply chains.

tension_points.bull_case: Demand exceeds supply, infrastructure is built to order, vacancy is at record lows, data-centre yields and cap rates are stable, and sentiment shows no widespread euphoria.
tension_points.bear_case: Capex/GDP rivals past booms, AI debt issuance is growing, the BIS warns of possible overcapacity, and financing and political constraints are building.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Supply starting to outstrip demand, which L&G says an end to the cycle would require.

tension_points.bull_case: Core inflation has probably peaked and the Fed will do less than the roughly 80bps priced, limited to reversing the 2025 insurance cuts.
tension_points.bear_case: Inflation remains stronger than policymakers want, with energy prices and AI capex keeping the market pricing hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Further energy price rises feeding a broader inflation shock.
